title: A quick threat model session
summary: Four questions applied to one feature.

steps.n: The team draws users, services, data stores and the lines between them, marking trust boundaries.
For each boundary crossing the team asks how it could be spoofed, tampered with, read or overloaded.
Each realistic threat gets a short sentence, such as a user changing an id in the URL to read another account.
A simple high, medium or low ranking decides what to deal with first.
Fix, reduce, accept or transfer. Every accepted risk has a named owner.
New features and integrations change the diagram, so the model is updated rather than filed away.

title: Handling a vulnerable dependency
summary: From a scanner finding to a safe release.

steps.n: The scanner reports that a library version has a known vulnerability, with a severity score.
The engineer checks if the vulnerable code is actually used and reachable. Severity alone is not the whole story.
The registry shows a patched version, and the release notes say if the update is compatible.
The version is raised in the lock file, and the test suite runs to catch breaking changes.
The pipeline repeats the scan on the new build and confirms the finding is gone.
The fix is released within the time the policy sets for that severity, and an exception is recorded if it cannot be.

title: From edit to commit
summary: How a change moves through the working tree, staging area and repository.

steps.n: You change a file in your working tree. Git notices the difference but has not saved anything yet.
Status lists the file as modified but not staged, so it would not be part of a commit right now.
The change is copied into the staging area, the draft of the next commit.
A second unrelated change stays in the working tree because you did not stage it.
Only the staged change becomes a permanent snapshot with a message, author and parent commit.
The branch pointer moves forward to the new commit, and the history grows by one step.
The unstaged change is untouched, ready to become a separate commit with its own message.

title: Branch and fast-forward merge
summary: Create a branch, commit on it and merge it back when main has not moved.

steps.n: The history is A, B and main points to B. You start from here.
A new pointer feature/retry is created at B. No files are copied, so it is instant.
You commit on the feature branch. The pointer feature/retry moves to C while main stays at B.
A second commit moves feature/retry to D. The work is isolated from main.
HEAD moves to main and the working files return to the state of B.
Main has not moved since the branch point, so Git only moves the main pointer forward to D.
History is a straight line A, B, C, D and no merge commit was created.
The merged branch label is deleted. The commits remain because main points to them.

title: Resolving a merge conflict
summary: Two branches change the same line and Git asks you to decide.

steps.n: You ask Git to merge the feature branch into main, which also changed the same file.
Git compares each branch with the common ancestor and finds two different edits to the same line.
The file now contains the markers with your version above the equals line and theirs below it.
Git reports the file and stops. The merge is in progress and git status shows both modified.
You decide the correct result, often a combination, and remove every marker line from the file.
Adding the file tells Git that this conflict is resolved.
Git creates the merge commit with two parents, finishing the merge.
A textually clean merge can still be logically wrong, so you test the combined result before pushing.

title: Rebase replays your commits
summary: Update a feature branch on the latest main by replaying commits.

steps.n: While you worked, teammates merged two new commits to main, so your branch is based on old code.
You ask Git to rebase. It remembers your commits, which are C and D.
Git sets your branch to the latest main commit, temporarily without your work.
The change of C is applied on top of main, creating a new commit with a different hash.
The change of D is applied next. If a conflict occurs, Git stops and asks you to resolve it.
Your branch now looks as if you started from the latest main, with no merge commit.
The rewritten branch must replace the remote copy, so you use force-with-lease on your own branch only.
Never rebase commits that other people have already pulled, because their copies would no longer match.

title: Fetch compared with pull
summary: What each command changes on your machine.

steps.n: You ask the server for new commits. Nothing in your working files changes.
The remote-tracking branch moves to the latest known server commit. This pointer is read-only.
You inspect what arrived before deciding how to integrate it.
If your main has no extra commits it moves forward to match. Otherwise Git refuses safely.
Pull is fetch followed by merge or rebase in one command, so the integration is automatic.
If both sides had new commits, a plain pull creates a merge commit that you did not ask for.
Setting pull.ff to only makes pull fail instead of surprising you, which pushes you to decide on purpose.

title: A rejected push
summary: Why a push fails and how to fix it without force.

steps.n: While you worked, the remote branch received a new commit that you do not have.
You try to publish your commits to the remote branch.
The remote branch has history that yours does not include, so a plain push would lose commit X.
You download the remote state to see exactly what is different.
You replay your commits on top of the colleague work, resolving conflicts if any.
You check that the combined code works, because both changes are now together.
The push is now a fast-forward of the remote branch, so the server accepts it.
A forced push would have discarded commit X. Force-with-lease is only for your own rewritten branches.

title: A pull request from start to merge
summary: The path of a change through branch, review, checks and merge.

steps.n: You branch from the latest main and make small commits with clear messages.

steps.l: Push and open a pull request
steps.n: The branch goes to the remote and a pull request describes what changed, why and how it was tested.
The pipeline runs lint, tests and security scans on the proposed result and reports status on the pull request.
The reviewer reads the change for correctness, safety and clarity and asks for changes where needed.
You push more commits or amend, the checks run again, and you ask for another look.
With checks green and the required approvals given, the merge button becomes available.
The platform merges by the chosen policy, squash, rebase or merge commit, into the protected main branch.
The merged commit triggers the build of one artifact that moves through the environments.

title: Reverting a shared commit
summary: Undo a bad change on main without rewriting history.

steps.n: After a deploy the error rate rises and the on-call engineer links it to the latest change.
git log shows the commit 7d1e0aa merged an hour ago, and others have already pulled it.
Git creates a new commit that applies the opposite change. Old history stays untouched.
The revert commit says why it exists and links the incident, so future readers understand.
The revert is reviewed and checked quickly, then merged, and everyone pulls it like any other commit.
The pipeline builds and deploys the fixed state, and the error rate returns to normal.
The original change is fixed on a new branch and re-applied with tests that cover the failure.

title: Recovering a lost commit
summary: Use the reflog after a hard reset.

steps.n: Your branch now points to a different commit, and the work you had committed seems to be gone.
The commit from yesterday is not listed because no branch points to it any more.
The reflog lists every place HEAD pointed, including the commit from before the reset.
You identify the entry that says commit: Tune ingress timeouts and copy its hash.
A new branch label is created at that commit, which makes it reachable again.
Garbage collection only removes unreachable commits, so a branch protects the work.
You bring the rescued work back into main with a merge or cherry-pick.
Uncommitted edits were never saved by Git, so the reflog cannot bring them back.

title: Finding the bad commit with bisect
summary: A binary search through 200 commits.

steps.n: You begin a bisect session and tell Git a bad commit (current) and a good one (v1.3.0).
Git picks the commit halfway between good and bad, leaving about 100 commits to examine.
Your script or a manual check shows whether this commit has the bug.
The bug is present here, so the first bad commit is in the earlier half. The range halves.
Git checks out a new middle commit, and the process repeats with 50, 25, 12 commits and so on.
The test passes on this one, so the problem was introduced later. The range keeps shrinking.
After about eight steps Git prints the commit that introduced the bug and its message.
You return to your original branch and use the finding to write the fix and a regression test.

title: A secret was committed
summary: The correct order of actions after a credential reaches the repository.

steps.n: The scanner flags an access key in a commit. You assume it is already copied.
You deactivate the key in the cloud account at once and issue a new one to the service.
You search for activity with the old key: new users, new keys, instances, data reads.
Anything the attacker created is deleted, and affected secrets are rotated.
git filter-repo removes the file from all commits, and the cleaned history is force-pushed.
Everyone re-clones or resets, because old clones and forks still contain the secret.
Push protection, pipeline scanning and a secret manager are enabled so the same mistake is blocked.
The team records what happened and what changed, without blaming a person.

title: Stash, hotfix and return
summary: Pause half-done work to ship an urgent fix.

steps.n: You have uncommitted edits on a feature branch when an urgent bug report arrives.
Your tracked changes are saved in the stash and the working tree is clean again.
A new branch starts from main so the fix is isolated from your unfinished feature.
You make the smallest correct change, run the tests and commit with a clear message.
The hotfix goes through a pull request and is merged to main, then deployed.
You return to your feature branch, which does not yet contain the hotfix.
The saved edits come back into the working tree and the stash entry is removed.
You rebase or merge main so your feature also has the fix before you continue.

title: Tag a release and ship a hotfix
summary: Annotated tags, artifacts and a fix for an older version.

steps.n: The release changes are merged to main and the tests pass.
An annotated tag marks the exact release commit with a message and the tagger.
CI builds one artifact from the tag and stamps the version and the commit hash into it.
The same artifact is promoted through the environments, so production runs exactly what was tested.
A defect is reported. You branch from the tag, not from main, so you fix only that version.
After the fix and tests, a new annotated tag is created. The old tag v1.4.0 is never moved.
The fix commit is copied to main, so the next release does not bring the bug back.

title: Faster clones for CI
summary: Shallow, partial and sparse clones cut the pipeline start time.

steps.n: A normal clone downloads every commit and file version, which for a large repository takes minutes.
All history arrives even though the job only builds the current code of one service.
The job asks for only the latest commit, so far fewer objects are transferred.
File contents are downloaded only when needed, instead of every version of every file.
Only the service folder and shared libraries appear in the working tree.
The first build step runs after a clone that takes seconds instead of minutes.
If a tool needs history, such as git describe, the job fetches more commits before it runs.

title: From go build to a running program
summary: How source files become one static binary and start running.

steps.n: The go command reads go.mod to find the module and the packages that the program imports.
Dependencies come from the module cache, and go.sum checksums are verified so downloaded code matches what was recorded.
Each package is compiled once and cached, so a rebuild only recompiles what changed.
The linker joins your code, dependencies and the Go runtime into one file with no separate runtime to install.
The result is a single file, static when CGO is disabled, which runs on a minimal container image.
Starting the file runs the runtime first, which sets up the scheduler and memory manager, then calls main.

title: How goroutines are scheduled
summary: How many goroutines share a few operating system threads.

steps.n: The go statement creates a goroutine with a small stack and hands it to the scheduler.

steps.l: Put it on a run queue
steps.n: New goroutines wait on a queue attached to a logical processor, ready to run.
The scheduler lets an operating system thread pick a goroutine and run it until it blocks or is preempted.
When a goroutine waits for a network read, the thread does not wait with it.
The scheduler parks the blocked goroutine and runs the next one from the queue on the same thread.
When the network data arrives, the goroutine becomes runnable again and continues where it stopped.

title: Channels hand off values safely
summary: How an unbuffered channel synchronises a sender and a receiver.

steps.n: The producer goroutine finishes some work and has a value ready.
The send blocks on an unbuffered channel until a receiver is ready, so both sides meet.
The consumer reaches the receive and the value is handed over directly.
Both goroutines continue. The hand-off also guarantees that writes before the send are visible after the receive.
The producer closes the channel when it has nothing more to send.
The consumer loop over the channel finishes when it is closed and empty, so it can exit cleanly.

title: Cancelling work with context
summary: How one cancellation stops every goroutine a request started.

steps.n: The handler derives a context with a deadline from the request context and defers cancel.
Each worker receives the context as its first parameter.
Both workers share the same cancellation signal.
After two seconds the context closes its Done channel and records the reason.
Worker A sees ctx.Done in its select and stops waiting on the slow call.
Worker B stops too, so no goroutine is left running for a request that has already failed.
The handler returns a timeout error to the client and the resources are released.

title: A request through net/http
summary: How a Go server routes and answers one HTTP request.

steps.n: The client connects and sends the request. The server runs each connection in its own goroutine.
net/http parses the method, path, headers and creates a request with a context.
The mux finds the handler registered for the method and path pattern.
The handler reads the path value, checks input and calls the store with the request context.
The handler sets the content type and writes the encoded response, handling encoding errors.
The response goes back. If the client disconnects, the request context is cancelled.

title: Graceful shutdown
summary: How a Go service finishes in-flight requests before exiting.

steps.n: The orchestrator asks the service to stop, usually with a grace period before killing it.
The readiness endpoint starts failing so the load balancer stops sending new requests.
Shutdown closes listeners and waits for active requests, up to a deadline.
The in-flight request completes normally and the connection closes.
A root context is cancelled so workers flush and stop.
The process exits cleanly before the grace period ends, with no dropped requests.

title: Wrapping and checking errors
summary: How context is added to an error without losing the cause.

steps.n: The standard library returns an error that wraps the system error for a missing file.
The service layer receives it and does not hide it.
Wrapping with the %w verb adds context and keeps the original error inside.
The handler receives an error whose message shows the full path of the failure.
The handler can still test for the original cause through the wrapping.
The error is logged at the edge with request details instead of at every layer.

title: A table-driven test run
summary: How go test runs many cases of one function.

steps.n: go test builds the package with its test files and calls each function that starts with Test.
The test holds a slice of cases with a name, input and expected output.
Each case runs as a subtest, so failures name the exact case.
The subtest checks the result and calls t.Errorf when it differs.
Results are collected per subtest and shown with -v.
Adding flags checks data races and reports which lines the tests touched.

title: A data race and its fix
summary: How two goroutines corrupt a counter and how a mutex fixes it.

steps.n: Goroutine A reads the value before incrementing.
Goroutine B reads the same value at the same moment.
Goroutine A writes six back to the counter.
B also writes six, so one increment is lost. This is a data race.
With a mutex, A takes the lock first and B has to wait.
After A unlocks, B sees six and writes seven. Run go test -race to catch the unsafe version.

title: A multi-stage Go image
summary: How a Go program ends up in a tiny container.

steps.n: The first stage has the full toolchain needed to compile.
Copying the module files first lets Docker reuse the download layer when only code changes.
The program is compiled into a static binary with no external libraries.
Only the binary is copied into the final image.
The final image runs as a non-root user on a minimal base such as distroless.
The result is tens of megabytes, which pulls and starts quickly.

title: Profiling a slow Go service
summary: How pprof shows where CPU time goes.

steps.n: Dashboards show the service using more CPU for the same traffic.
The engineer requests a CPU profile from the internal debug port during load.
The runtime samples call stacks about 100 times per second for the duration.
Wide boxes show functions that use the most time.

steps.l: Find JSON encoding in a loop
steps.n: The widest box is repeated encoding of the same value, which can be cached.
After the change a new profile shows the box gone and CPU use down.

title: How a goroutine leaks
summary: How an abandoned sender blocks forever and memory grows.

steps.n: The handler starts a goroutine that will send its result on an unbuffered channel.
The handler gives up after a timeout and returns an error to the client.
The slow call completes after the handler is gone.
The send waits for a receiver that will never come.
Every timed-out request leaves one blocked goroutine, so memory grows steadily.
Using select on ctx.Done and a buffer of one lets the worker exit and the count stays flat.

title: Modules and go.sum
summary: How Go verifies dependencies.

steps.n: A dependency is added with an exact version in go.mod.
The go command fetches the module, usually through a proxy.
The content hash is written to go.sum.
Both files are committed so every machine builds the same code.
On another machine, the downloaded content must match the recorded hash.
If the content differs, the build stops, which protects against tampered or changed modules.

title: What helm install does
summary: From command to objects running in the cluster.

steps.n: The command names the release, the chart and the values files.
Chart defaults, values files and --set flags are merged in order of priority.
The templates are rendered into plain Kubernetes manifests using the merged values.
Helm sends the rendered objects to the API server using your kubeconfig.
The release record with chart, values and manifest is stored as a Secret in the namespace.
The cluster creates the objects and pods start. helm status shows the release as deployed.

title: An atomic upgrade that rolls back
summary: How --atomic protects a release from a bad rollout.

steps.n: The pipeline asks for an upgrade that must become healthy before it counts as done.
Helm records a new revision as pending-upgrade.
The Deployment is updated and new pods start with the new image.
The new pods never become ready, because the app crashes on startup.
After the timeout Helm re-applies the manifest of revision 4.
The pipeline fails while the site keeps serving the old version.

title: How values are merged
summary: Which setting wins when several sources provide the same key.

steps.n: The chart supplies a default for every setting it supports.
The environment file overrides the default for production.
A --set flag on the command line has the highest priority and wins.
The chart default list has two hosts.
The environment list replaces the whole default list, not just one item.
After installing, this command shows exactly which values were used.

title: Rendering a template
summary: How curly braces become YAML.

steps.n: The template contains a placeholder for the value.
The engine reads the value from the merged settings.
Functions such as default, quote and toYaml transform values.
Dashes in braces remove blank lines and keep the indentation valid.
The result is a plain Kubernetes manifest with no braces left.
Running helm template prints the result so you can check it before applying.

title: Rolling back a release
summary: How a rollback creates a new revision from an older one.

steps.n: The engineer lists revisions and finds the last good one, revision 7.
Helm loads the stored manifest and values of that revision.
The rollback command is issued and waits for readiness.
The objects are patched back to the state described in revision 7.
A new revision is stored. History only grows.
The previous version serves traffic again. Data changes are not undone.

title: Why secrets do not belong in values
summary: Where a password in values ends up.

steps.n: A password is committed in a values file.
Deleting the line later does not remove it from past commits and clones.
The value is passed to the chart and stored in the release Secret.
Anyone who can read the release Secret can print the password.
Treat the secret as exposed and change it.
The chart now takes only the name of a Secret created by a secret manager.

title: Updating chart dependencies
summary: How a subchart is pinned and fetched.

steps.n: The chart lists the dependency with a version and a repository.
Helm fetches the exact version from the repository or registry.
The package is stored in the charts folder of your chart.
The lock file records the exact version and a digest.
Committing the lock keeps builds repeatable.
CI rebuilds from the lock and does not pick up unreviewed updates.

title: Publishing a chart to an OCI registry
summary: From chart folder to a versioned package.

steps.n: The chart is packed into a versioned .tgz file.
Helm authenticates to the registry.
The package is uploaded as an OCI artifact next to container images.
The registry keeps the version and can sign or scan it.
A cluster pipeline pulls the exact version.
The pipeline now installs the same package that was reviewed.

title: A pre-upgrade migration hook
summary: How a Job runs before the new version starts.

steps.n: Helm renders all templates, including those marked as hooks.
The hook Job is created before the other objects are changed.
The Job runs the migration against the database.
Helm waits for the Job and continues only if it succeeded.
Now the new application version is rolled out.
A delete policy cleans up the finished Job. A failed hook stops the whole upgrade.

title: A release stuck in pending-upgrade
summary: How an interrupted job blocks later deployments.

steps.n: The pipeline begins an upgrade.
Helm stores the new revision in a pending state.
The CI runner is terminated before Helm finishes.
A later pipeline run starts another upgrade.
Helm refuses because the last revision never finished.
The engineer rolls back to the last deployed revision, which resets the state, and the next upgrade works.

title: Running helm test
summary: How a smoke test pod checks a release.

steps.n: After a deploy, the engineer or pipeline asks Helm to run the chart tests.
Helm creates the Pod marked with the test hook.
The test pod calls the application the way a client would.
A healthy application answers.
The pod exits successfully and Helm reports the test as passed.
A failed test fails the job and can trigger a rollback.
